# The Gear Ratio Trade-off: Why Fewer Speeds Matter More Than You Think

Choosing between a four-speed and a five, six, or seven-speed automatic transmission isn't just about marketing numbers; it fundamentally alters how an engine interacts with the road. When comparing a 1.6-liter engine paired with a four-speed automatic against modern equivalents, the discrepancy lies in gear ratio spread and torque multiplication.

In a multi-gear system, each gear represents a specific ratio between engine RPM and wheel rotation. A wider range of gears allows the transmission to keep the engine operating within its optimal power band across varying speeds. With only four ratios available, the gaps between them become significantly larger. This forces the engine to climb higher in RPMs to achieve highway velocities or drop lower during deceleration, often resulting in inefficient fuel consumption and reduced acceleration capability.

### Top Speed and Motorway Performance

Your concern regarding top speed on a motorway is partially valid but depends heavily on the final drive ratio and the engine's peak power output. In most modern vehicles, a four-speed automatic will not physically prevent you from reaching 120 km/h or even 140 km/h if the engine has enough torque to overcome aerodynamic drag at those speeds.

However, "reaching" the speed limit is different from maintaining it efficiently. Because there are fewer ratios, the fifth gear in a five-speed unit often serves as an overdrive ratio (where output RPM is lower than input RPM). In a four-speed setup, the fourth gear might still be close to 1:1 or even slightly underdriven at highway speeds. This means your engine will spin faster to maintain 120 km/h compared to a vehicle with more gears.

The consequence is higher fuel consumption and increased heat generation in the transmission. While you won't hit a hard electronic limiter preventing you from going fast, you will be working the engine harder than necessary. If the 1.6-liter engine in your shortlisted Toyota Corolla Altis lacks sufficient torque at high RPMs—a common trait of older naturally aspirated engines designed for this era—the vehicle may struggle to sustain higher speeds without feeling strained.

### Acceleration and Overtaking Dynamics

The issue with acceleration is far more pronounced than top speed limitations. Fewer gears mean fewer opportunities to shift down quickly when you need extra power.

Consider the scenario of overtaking on a highway. You accelerate from 80 km/h to 100 km/h, then floor it for the pass. In a five-speed or six-speed transmission, the system can drop into third gear almost instantly, providing an immediate surge of torque. With only four gears, the gap between second and fourth is massive. The transmission must hold the car in second gear longer to build speed, keeping RPMs high but lacking the leverage needed for rapid acceleration.

This explains why your experience with the 1.3-liter manual felt acceptable while the search results suggest the 1.3-liter automatic was underpowered. A manual gearbox allows you to manually select the optimal gear before shifting, whereas an early four-speed automatic relies on a hydraulic or electronic logic that may be conservative in its shift points to protect the transmission from overspinning. The smaller engine exacerbates this; less torque at the crankshaft means the limited ratios cannot compensate effectively.

### Efficiency and Real-World Usage

Since your primary use is city driving, you might assume four gears are sufficient for stop-and-go traffic. In reality, fewer gears often hurt city efficiency more than they help. Modern engines rely on low-ratio gearing to maximize torque delivery at lower speeds without stalling or lugging. A fourth gear in a 2000s-era transmission is rarely as tall (numerically lower) as a fifth or sixth gear found in newer cars.

This results in the engine running at higher RPMs during normal city cruising, burning more fuel and creating more noise and vibration. The lack of an overdrive ratio forces the engine to operate less efficiently than it could if it had access to five distinct steps between idle and maximum speed.

If you are deciding between the Toyota Corolla Altis with its four-speed automatic and a competitor like the Honda City, prioritize the transmission count unless the older car offers significantly better build quality or reliability history that outweighs the performance deficit. The extra gear in modern transmissions is not just an added feature; it is essential for matching engine output to road demands efficiently. Unless you have specific data showing the 1.6-liter model compensates perfectly with superior tuning, the five-speed alternative will likely provide a smoother, more responsive driving experience without the fuel penalty.
